text: This lab traces a 2-layer, 2-qubit QNN-style circuit's forward pass by hand, encoding, two rotation-plus-entangling blocks, and measurement, closing out the chapter by making the QNN label fully concrete on an actual multi-qubit example.

Two qubits start at zero-zero. Layer 1 applies RY of pi over 2 to qubit 1, giving 0.7071, 0.7071, and RY of pi over 3 to qubit 2, giving 0.8660, 0.5000, then a CNOT with qubit 1 as control. Before entangling, the combined tensor-product state has amplitudes 0.6124, 0.3536, 0.6124, 0.3536 across the four basis states, checking out to exactly 1.0000 normalized.

Here's a precise, verified fact. Qubit 1, the control, keeps an expectation value of cosine of pi over 2, exactly zero, completely unchanged by the CNOT — a CNOT never alters its control qubit's own marginal probabilities. Qubit 2, the target, tells a different story: before the CNOT its expectation value was cosine of pi over 3, 0.5000, but after the CNOT it drops to exactly 0.0000, a real, computed change caused entirely by entangling it with qubit 1.

Adding a second rotation layer, theta three equals pi over 5, theta four equals pi over 7, followed by a second CNOT, gives an expectation value on qubit 1 of about negative 0.5090, and on qubit 2 of about 0.6195. Neither number matches any calculation using only one qubit's own parameters — both now depend on the full set of four parameters, mixed together by two rounds of entanglement.

Chapter 5 opens next by naming explicitly the hybrid classical-quantum structure that's been implicit in every lab so far, tracing exactly where control passes between classical and quantum code during training.
